text: A new scoped application is created through Studio, ServiceNow's dedicated development environment. You get there from System Applications, then Studio, then Create Application — the real, intended entry point, and also where you'll spend most of Chapters 5 through 9 of this course once the application exists, building tables, Business Rules, Script Includes, and UI Pages inside it.

Choosing Create Application walks you through a short wizard. Two fields on that wizard matter far more than the rest, and one of them deserves real caution before you type anything: Scope ID, which is the application's display name, and Version, which tracks its lifecycle.

Scope ID is the source of the application's permanent scope identifier — the prefix baked into every table and field name the application will ever create. Pick a name like Fleet Management, and Studio derives an identifier like x_acme_fleet. A reasonable naming convention follows the pattern vendor prefix plus short app name: x_acme_fleet for Fleet Management, x_acme_vms for Visitor Management. Avoid generic names like x_acme_app1 that won't mean anything to the next developer reading x_acme_app1_vehicle six months from now.

Here's the caution: the scope identifier cannot be changed after the application is created. This isn't a UI limitation someone might fix later — it's structural. The identifier gets woven into the real name of every table, field, and Script Include call the moment they're created inside that application. Decide your naming convention before you click Create Application, not after.

Renaming a scope after the fact would mean renaming every table, every field reference in every script, and every Script Include call across the entire application — not a safe or supported operation. The Version field, meanwhile, tracks application lifecycle: what's been published, and later, what's running where if the application is ever packaged for distribution. This course doesn't go deep on publishing — that's beyond this course's scope — but the field exists from the moment of creation.

The moment the application is created, Studio generates a new sys_scope record and immediately sets up that application's file structure — the organized container every table, Business Rule, Script Include, and UI Page you build from this point forward will be filed under. Lesson 22 covers that structure in depth. For now, know this organization starts the instant the application exists, not after you've built a few things and asked for it. Next up: the real mechanisms for letting one scope reach into another, safely.
